title: Across 100 runs, our KYC and KYB agents reached the same verdict every time

body_markdown:
### Where the evidence was clear, the answer never changed. Where it wasn't, variations were inconsequential to the result.


Given the same case, does an agent reach the same conclusion every time? Non-deterministic systems make that question hard, and a regulated file makes it unavoidable. We tested our KYC and KYB agents to find out.


We ran ten cases, five individuals and five companies, ten times each under a frozen configuration. We graded each of the 100 runs independently against a written ground truth and compared it only with other runs of the same case.


Every verdict resting on a hard, well-evidenced fact held at 10 of 10. In every run, the agent distinguished case subjects from public figures who shared their names. Variance appeared only in judgment-based severity calls, and each instance traced to an identifiable cause.


### Why repeatability matters


Most agent evaluation asks whether a single run got the right answer. An examiner needs more: the same answer months later. An agent that returns "warning" today and "hard fail" on the identical case tomorrow creates a procedural problem even if both verdicts are defensible, because a regulated file claims a repeatable process, not a lucky run.


### How we ran it


Individuals ran through the KYC skill stack: address verification, source of wealth, industry risk, geographic risk, adverse media, sanctions, and political exposure. Companies ran through the KYB stack, which adds registration verification, company source of wealth, and four web-presence checks: content review, domain history, online reputation, and terms and conditions.


The cases paired easy inputs with hard ones. A thin-file identity sat against a name that collides with a well-known public figure. A registered-agent mail-forwarding address sat against a landmark commercial building used as a home address. A dual-use, high-risk technology operator sat against a plain manufacturer, and a dormant shell sat against a company with a confirmed public fraud history.


Before any run, we recorded each skill's expected verdict and the fact pattern that justified it. We merged WARN and INFO into one bucket, since both mean the skill reached neither a clean pass nor a confirmed fail. The configuration was frozen, but the environment was not. Sanctions search and registration lookup return different results for identical queries, and the test measured that too.


### Where the agent was consistent


Hard facts never moved. A dissolved entity's closed registry status produced the same registration verdict in every run. A company's confirmed fraud and liquidation history matched on adverse media every time. A mail-forwarding suite failed address verification in all ten runs, and the geocode never persuaded the skill it was a residence. A dual-use technology operator failed the same industry-risk rule ten of ten times.


The name-collision cases held too. Two individual profiles shared a name with a real public figure, paired with a date of birth built to contradict that person's identity. In all 20 runs, the agent flagged the name-only match and the conflicting date of birth. It logged an unverifiable identity rather than attributing someone else's public record to the case. That separates a defensible disposition from a serious false attribution.


### Where it varied, and why


Variance came from classification, not facts. On the same evidence, severity calls moved for three reasons. Absence-of-evidence defaults were applied inconsistently. A severity mapping read the same baseline "High Risk" match as a warning in some runs and a hard fail in others. The sanctions and registration tools themselves behaved nondeterministically. None was an unexplained flip, so each has a fix: tighten the default, sharpen the threshold, stabilize the tool. Variance you can explain is variance you can remove.


### The bottom line


Repeatability does not replace accuracy. An agent that is confidently wrong ten times out of ten is still wrong, and we grade correctness separately. But when an agent's output goes into a regulated file, repeatability is part of the claim you make about the system, and you have to measure it on purpose.


If you are deploying agents into compliance or financial operations, we should talk.
